title: Ang 609–630: Guru Arjan in Sorath
hookLine: one Father, all His children, on ang 611
tomorrow: who can feel pain and still not be ruled by it?

lines: THE GUEST LIST IS A MAP.
cards: A wedding guest list is a map of who counts. Cousins, yes. Second cousins, maybe.
Dad's old coworker, the neighbors, the bride's friends from work who've never set foot in a gurdwara. Somebody always asks where the line is.
On ang 611, Guru Arjan answers yesterday's question without drawing one: there is one Father, and we are all children of the One.

teach.h: ONE FATHER, CHILDREN OF THE ONE.
teach.b: Guru Arjan's Sorath hymns run across these pages, and this one is the heart of the day. In paraphrase: one Father, and we are the children of the One; you are our Guru.
Then it turns tender: listen, friend, I'd give myself for you; show me the sight of the Lord. So the family line isn't a fence.

teach.h: NOT A FENCE: WHERE WE CAME FROM.
teach.b: It's a picture of where everyone came from. Here's a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN: SO YOU MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another."
Shared: one human family from one source, and our differences as a reason to meet.
One honest difference: the Qur'an doesn't speak of God as a father.
It speaks of the Creator who made people from a pair and spread them into peoples, and the same verse goes on to say the noblest in God's sight is the best in conduct.

Guru Arjan's picture is a household, one Father and his children, and his hymn moves from family into longing to see God. Two ways of saying it, each in its own voice. Neither one says the traditions are the same.

how: Sikhs often recite 'ek pita ekas ke ham barik' from Guru Arjan's Sorath hymn on ang 611 when speaking of one human family; gurdwaras welcome guests of any background, who cover their heads like everyone else.

games.q: at a dinner, someone says, 'if we're all one family, then all religions must be teaching the same thing.' what fits today?
o: one human family, yes; but each tradition says it its own way, with real differences.
yes, exactly; the differences between religions are just words.
no; only one tradition can really mean we're one family.
games.why: Guru Arjan says one Father and his children; the Qur'an says one Creator who made nations to know one another, and doesn't call God father. close, not the same, and nobody ranked.

practice: Look at one group photo, on your phone or on a wall: a class, a team, a family gathering. Let your eyes rest on each face in turn, including the ones you barely know.
Stay with the photo for the sit, and let Guru Arjan's picture sit over all of them: children of the One.
